findings.finding: The plan assumes `timeout 300 docker exec ... --refresh-code` actually bounds the refresh. When timeout kills the docker exec client, the process started inside the container is typically not signalled. It keeps running, along with its git fetch and the code-checkout directory lock it holds (fd 9 flock). The plan doesn't confirm that the in-container refresh ends when the timeout fires, or say what happens when it doesn't. If it doesn't, the next tick's refresh blocks waiting for that lock (MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT defaults to 7200 s) until its own timeout fires, and the same thing repeats on every tick after that.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Enforce the 300 s bound inside the container, not just on the host's docker exec client, so a hung fetch can't leave an orphaned refresh holding the code-checkout lock.
evidence: autodeploy.sh:712: `if timeout 300 docker exec "$name" sh /usr/local/bin/mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code`
mcp-entrypoint.sh:231: refresh_code runs under `with_dir_lock "$code_dir" "code checkout" refresh_code_locked`; lock acquisition waits only until a deadline and then returns 1
Killing a docker exec client does not signal the exec'd process inside the container
findings.finding: The plan says the refresh is 'bounded at 300 s, like the mirror fetch', but the bound wraps the host-side `docker exec` client. When `timeout` kills that client, the process inside the container (the entrypoint holding the checkout flock, plus its git fetch or merge) keeps running. A hung remote leaves an orphaned refresh that holds the code-checkout lock indefinitely. Later refreshes, and any container-start provisioning that shares the lock, then fail to get it until their wait deadline. The mirror fetch runs on the host, so its timeout really does kill git; the analogy doesn't carry over.
findings.location: Approach — 'bounded at 300 s, like the mirror fetch'; infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:712-713; infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh:128-141 (with_dir_lock)
scenarios: GitHub stalls mid-fetch: autodeploy times out after 300 s and moves on, but the in-container git fetch hangs, still holding the checkout lock; every later tick's refresh fails at lock acquisition and the workspace stays stale until the container restarts.
A blue-green start of a new container whose provisioning shares the checkout inode blocks or fails on the orphan's lock.
findings.suggested_fix: Run the timeout inside the container, e.g. `timeout 310 docker exec "$name" timeout 300 sh /usr/local/bin/mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code` (keeping the outer host bound slightly larger). Alternatively, set git's own stall limits for the refresh fetch (GIT_HTTP_LOW_SPEED_LIMIT / GIT_HTTP_LOW_SPEED_TIME). Add a test where the stubbed in-container refresh hangs, and assert that it is terminated and the lock is released.

findings.finding: The '300 s bound' wraps the host-side `docker exec` client. Killing that client when the timeout fires does not stop the `mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code` process inside the container. A hung in-container `git fetch origin main` therefore keeps running and keeps holding the code-checkout flock after autodeploy has moved on. The deploy lock is freed, but the work is not bounded and the orphaned process can block later refresh attempts until the lock wait times out.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Bound the refresh inside the container: run the `timeout` within the `docker exec` and cap the lock wait (e.g. `MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT`), confirm that a timed-out refresh leaves no orphaned process in the container, and add a test for it.
evidence: Plan: "runs `docker exec <live> sh /usr/local/bin/mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code` (bounded at 300 s, like the mirror fetch)"
autodeploy.sh:712: `if timeout 300 docker exec "$name" \` — the timeout wraps the docker CLI client, not the in-container command
autodeploy.sh:553: the mirror fetch wraps `git` directly (`timeout "$FETCH_TIMEOUT" git -C ... fetch`), so the two are not 'like' each other
mcp-entrypoint.sh:15: `MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT="${MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT:-7200}"`; the refresh waits up to 2 h for the checkout lock inside the container

Evidence class: Partially-verified. `docker exec` is an existing integration, but the claimed 'bounded' behaviour (timeout killing the in-container process) is unverified and contradicts known Docker exec signal semantics. Confirm empirically: `timeout 2 docker exec <c> sleep 60`, then `docker top <c>`.
findings.finding: The 'bounded at 300 s, like the mirror fetch' claim relies on `timeout` stopping the in-container refresh, and it doesn't. `timeout 300 docker exec <live> sh .../mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code` signals only the host-side `docker exec` CLI. Docker does not pass that signal on to, or kill, the process started inside the container when the exec client dies (a long-standing Docker limitation; `docker run`'s sig-proxy has no `docker exec` equivalent). The mirror fetch is different: there `timeout` kills git itself. So on a hung remote the deploy lock is released, but the in-container `git fetch origin main` keeps running and keeps the code-checkout flock. Each later tick then starts another exec that waits up to `MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT=7200` s for that lock, piling up orphaned processes inside the live MCP container.
findings.location: Approach — infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh `mcp_refresh_code_workspace` (autodeploy.sh:712-713); infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh `with_dir_lock`/`MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT` (lines 15, 128-141)
scenarios: GitHub or the network stalls mid-fetch: the host `timeout` fires after 300 s, but the in-container git keeps running and keeps the checkout lock.

The next no-op ticks (every few minutes) each start another `docker exec ... --refresh-code` that blocks on the lock for up to 7200 s inside the container, so stuck sh/python3/git processes build up in the live MCP backend while it serves traffic.
An interrupted-but-not-killed refresh stays alive alongside a later container-start `refresh_code`, so the recovery path runs later than the plan assumes.
findings.suggested_fix: Run the bound inside the container, e.g. `timeout 310 docker exec -e MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT=60 "$name" timeout 300 sh /usr/local/bin/mcp-entrypoint.sh --refresh-code`. The inner `timeout` kills the in-container process tree, the outer one stays as a backstop for a hung docker daemon, and the short lock wait stops a later tick from queueing behind a stuck peer for 2 h. First confirm that `timeout` (coreutils) exists in the MCP image, or fall back to git's own limits (`-c http.lowSpeedLimit=1 -c http.lowSpeedTime=60`).
